title: Nation Media Group: The Editors Who Shaped It
content:
Nation Media Group began in 1959 as a small Swahili newspaper bought by the newly installed Aga Khan IV, then grew into East and Central Africa’s largest independent media house. Its story is inseparable from Kenya’s own: the making of a nation, the defence of a public sphere, and now the struggle to preserve that public sphere in a digital, politically pressured age. 




From Taifa to Nation




The founding transaction was modest: in 1959, Prince Karim Aga Khan IV bought 

Taifa

, a Kiswahili weekly, from former District Commissioner Charles Hayes and his business partner Althea Tebbut for £10,000. The company behind it, East African Newspapers (Nation Series) Ltd., was formed on April 2, 1959.




Taifa

 became 

Taifa Leo

 in January 1960; the 

Sunday Nation

 followed in March and the 

Daily Nation

 in October that year. By the time Kenya attained independence in December 1963, the Nation had already established itself as a credible source of news and analysis.




Its founding purpose was more than commercial. NMG describes its origin as an effort to give voice to African Kenyans in the final years of colonial rule, while the Aga Khan’s stated ambition was to help build a free, independent press capable of supporting democratic governance.

title: The Decline of The Nation: From Taifa to Taarifa
content:
When I worked at the Nation Media Group (NMG), there was a running joke about the immortality of 

Taifa Leo

, the Swahili newspaper printed by the media group that 20-year-old Prince Karim had bought in 1959 when he became the Fourth Aga Khan.




From this £10,000 purchase from British officer and former District Commissioner Charles Hayes, the group would grow to control the largest circulation of newspapers, and television stations and websites across East Africa.




Over time, the Swahili paper did face dwindling audiences as demographic changes produced a more cosmopolitan youth who found reading news in grammatical Swahili a hard sell and was more inclined to consume short video content online. 




Despite this handicap, 

Taifa Leo

 owes its longevity to the sentimental connection to its founder, His Highness the Aga Khan. For its survival, it also relied on punchy yet witty headlines, humorous angles, and 

Bi Taifa

, a cover model featured on one of its pages that was primarily produced by Taifa Leo photographers. If you hung around these photographers long enough, you would get to see how the allure of appearing on the tabloid would create new customers looking out for their photos. 




Then the Fourth Aga Khan died, and 

Taifa Leo

’s business model was finally facing the test of succession, a shift in the media landscape, and an uncertain future under Tanzanian billionaire Rostam Aziz who may share the paper’s Swahili heritage but not the paper’s founding ideals that had inspired its punchy headlines. 




Succession




The Fourth Aga Khan’s strategy with 

Taifa Leo

 was to create a sustainable, independent, and influential media platform that would inform the public and strengthen the fabric of the newly independent nation.




A younger Aga Khan had borne the cost of the loss-making venture in its first decade and had 

fought off attempts

 by the family of Kenya’s first president, Jomo Kenyatta, to gain control of the media house and turn it into an organ of state propaganda. 




But as the Aga Khan grew older and gradually relinquished his stake to other shareholders and to a professional board, this legacy of defending the sanctity of media freedom began to wane. 




Under the younger Kenyatta, the old Aga Khan’s legacy project 

gave in to state interference

 in what could be linked to privileges and immunities granted to the Aga Khan Development Network (AKDN) and its affiliated agencies, which were classified as philanthropic, charitable and non-profit-making.




But even tax exemptions and the economies of scale of running Aga Khan’s conglomerates across East Africa could not save the businesses’ fortunes and their decline in profitability would lead to divestments under his son, Prince Rahim Al-Hussaini, the Fifth Aga Khan, shortly after the patriarch’s death.




Shifting landscapes




I owe a huge part of my journalism career to the late Prince Karim Aga Khan, having worked at Nation Media Group where I learned the trade until I transitioned into private practice a couple of years ago.




But even as I transitioned out, I was still a beneficiary of his benevolence when I enlisted for a course titled “Beyond the Newsroom” that aimed to help journalists move on following the job cuts that had become the norm in the industry.




This programme demonstrated that the Aga Khan understood the dynamics of our evolving media industry and had chosen to help incubate future media start-ups through the Aga Khan University Graduate School of Media and Communications.




I found myself sitting in a lecture hall where two of the trainers now teaching journalists how to cope beyond the newsroom had been the managers who had hired me into the profession.




David Aduda had hired me at the Nation Media Group in 2013, then three years later, Joseph Odindo poached me to join Standard Media Group. But they were now both with the Aga Khan University School of Media, providing sponsored training to the scores of journalists made redundant by the decline of traditional media.




Golden age




I muscled my way into journalism as a fresh graduate from Maseno University, moving to the capital and into a profession that was brimming with opportunity.




In 2013, Kenya was undergoing a rather calm political transition and the world had forgotten about the financial crisis. Anything seemed possible, including printing money.




I first interned at the NMG when it was making KSh13.3 billion in revenues and netting KSh2.5 billion in profits. You can imagine my surprise when, after undergoing intense interviews, psychometric tests, and questions about quantitative easing (the new name of printing money), I was handed a KSh7,000 contract.




But I believed in the calling. I remember visiting the Kenya Television Network as a member of the Debate and Journalism club while in high school, and the Nation Centre when I was a university student, and telling myself that one day I would work where once Whispers had worked; he fascinated me when I was young. I lived in a derelict building somewhere in Kariobangi where the rent was KSh5,000, but I still signed on the dotted line and then convinced my father and my sister to underwrite the risk.




It paid off; I walked into a vibrant newsroom and got to meet and work with Ken Walibora. I sat in that part of the newsroom known as “Migingo”, the desks nearest those of Ugandans Onyango Obbo and Daniel Kalinaki. Back then the newsroom was so vibrant it scouted universities for the best talent to bring into its media lab programme – writers like Jacqueline Kubania, Cornell Ngare, and Waga Odongo.




Decline




I tell anyone who cares to listen that I have witnessed the industry transform. At the time, we interns were not assigned computers, so we would hang around, sitting on the chairs meant for the group’s drivers, waiting for “Mayor of Migingo” John Ngirachu to leave for parliament, or for some other senior journalist to go for an assignment, and pounce on their desks to write those little briefs whose authorship no one knew.




But by the time I left the newsroom, I was surrounded by four empty desks; I could have written an introduction at one and concluded my story at another of those unused workstations where once such and such a colleague used to sit. Where are they now? 




I met some of them while attending the Beyond the Newsroom training; right in front of me on the very first day were Aduda and Odindo. They had transitioned themselves and were now passing on their wealth of experience to us.




I had attended Odindo’s leaving party and had felt at the time that this was what media success looked like; the charming speeches celebrated him, and he seemed almost agreeable to what was an inevitable goodbye.




Business convergence, digital reorganizations




Since then journalists have not been given such lavish send-offs. Their departures have instead been announced by internal memo or through the regular cycles of redundancies, business convergence, and all manner of digital reorganizations. Exits have become a source of industry anxiety; the despair, the uncertainty and the anger at having loved a dog’s life and being rejected via a cursory letter, a phone call, a disabled email address, or a cancelled entry pass.




It turns out Odindo took it just as hard as the rest of us when we left the newsroom. He made a short return to the industry at the 

Standard

 before joining the Aga Khan Media School as a trainer. Through it all, the lesson for the veteran had been to remember who he really was – a good editor who did his work diligently, managing other editors and overseeing a newsroom over the years – and therein lay his strength.




And as he sought himself in the shock therapy that is retirement, digging through piles of old documents, the words of a distant headmaster on his report card saying, “Joseph is capable of much more” lent him the courage to try new things.




But tell that to a pack of depressed former journalists thrown into the tailspin of sudden joblessness – the struggle to pay rent and school fees, learning to take rejection from job applications, being worried sick about lacking insurance and, above all, losing the power and privileges that come with working for a huge news organization. Journalism is a strange profession, built around the façade of the glamorous television anchors, powerful owners, backed by human rights defenders and international patronage. But once you step off, the entire network freezes you out.




But even in the midst of this despair, a group of journalists attending the training found solace in each other’s company, sharing their experiences, their unvoiced emotions. As we shared our stories and learned the limitations of our mindsets to our present careers, the opportunities available to our skill sets and, really thinking about our industry, it became apparent why the Aga Khan’s initiative to help transition the industry was so important.




Structured monopoly




Prince Karim Aga Khan, who grew up in Nairobi and founded the 

Daily Nation

 in the 1960s, has for decades underwritten media freedom and its success in Kenya, using his financial muscle to shoulder the capital-intensive business and leveraging its power to support his massive business ventures in hospitality, energy, agriculture, insurance, and finance. 




The newspaper model had, over the years, become archaic, relying on central printing and physical distribution through an expensive logistical network. This costly structure acted as an entry barrier, making the industry a near monopoly for those who could afford to own it.




The internet completely disrupted this distribution model, replacing the newspaper with a mobile telephone and a computer screen that virtually made anyone with an internet connection a potential journalist. This happened at a time when America was printing money through quantitative easing, which was funnelled to tech companies to finance experiments on customer targeting. The social media model that allowed companies to study the individual and influence their behaviour changed how advertising was done and the role of the media as gatekeeper of audiences. Social media ate legacy media’s lunch, and as advertising revenues dropped, the cost of maintaining media operations became increasingly high. Media houses reacted by cutting costs and trimming staff numbers.




The Nation Group’s profits have been in sharp decline, falling from KSh2.5 billion when I joined the company in 2013 to a loss of KSh308.6 million in 2025. In the same period, the group’s staff nearly halved – from 1,980 to 

1,100

 – due to the annual ritual of rationalization that has only served to heighten anxiety in the newsroom.




“We were too busy doing the traditional thing. We knew about the disruptions from technology but were engrossed in the product to make money for the employer that we ignored digital. We were so engrossed in competition for the little space doing what we had done for so long,” Odindo told us during the training.




Now digital is viewed as the magic bullet even though newsrooms know that the same technology is spelling their end. 




“Notwithstanding the operating performance for the period, the gains recorded in digital and broadcasting underscore the Group’s sustained pivot toward a scalable digital business and optimization of the growth headroom in broadcasting. Therefore, the Group continues to invest in unified technology to enhance customer experience across our platforms, diversify audience demographics and accelerate monetization of our expansive digital assets,” the 

Nation

’s board of directors said in its 2025 results outlook.




Business interests 




It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest. As the media business shrank, so did the interest of its benevolent founder. 




Even as the newspaper model began to collapse, the Aga Khan’s interests shifted elsewhere – to his multiple businesses that include the Aga Khan Hospital, the TPS Serena hotel chain, Jubilee Insurers and Diamond Trust Bank, IPSK and Farmers Choice, and power stations. He sought to secure tax concessions for them at the expense of media independence. 




Inevitably, politicians took advantage of the dire straits in which the media found itself, using advertising revenues to leverage friendly coverage. The government weaponized media revenues, using its power as the largest advertiser to accumulate invoices that crippled the newsrooms and then withholding advertising altogether before negotiating the cost of advertising downwards by having the leading newspapers carry the government’s 

MyGov

 pamphlet as an insert.




As the handshake extended beyond the elbow, so did the pressure to push out dissenting journalists like Dennis Galava and Godfrey Mwampembwa (Gaddo), which gave the Aga Khan a bad press for what was seen as giving in to the demands of a government averse to criticism. 




Like the Children of Gebelawi, we wondered what the Aga Khan thought as he watched the empire that he had built over decades go into decline.




Last man standing




After President Daniel Moi left office, fortunes at the 

Standard

 were not good either. Between 2024 and 2015, the firm only made profits twice in a decade as the losses widened to over a billion in the last years (KSh1.1 billion in 2024). In newsrooms, the Standard Group’s losses were glossed over while the company struggled to pay correspondents – contract writers who are paid by the length of each published article. The silence continued even as the late payment of salaries finally hit permanent staff and the industry slid slowly into the practice of not paying journalists on time and sometimes not at all.




The 

Standard

 newspaper blamed its troubles on the state’s non-payment of outstanding bills despite the fact that its owner, Gideon Moi, was part of President Uhuru Kenyatta’s inner circle in Azimio.




Despite the dip in fortunes, the paper has maintained its relevance through bold headlines critical of President William Ruto’s regime to recover falling circulation. The newspaper gives Gideon Moi leverage in shaping public opinion. He is reported to have 

turned down

 an offer from Ruto’s allies who had been seeking to acquire a stake in the struggling Standard Group.




According to Africa Intelligence, President Ruto then turned his 

sights on NMG

, having bagged 

The Star

 to start building a media empire through which to control the narrative ahead of the 2027 presidential election.




With the Aga Khan Fund for Economic Development agreeing to sell its entire 

shareholding in NPRT Holdings Africa Limited

 to Taarifa Limited, which is owned by Tanzanian Business Magnate Rostam Aziz, many see this as the takeover of East Africa’s most powerful media house by politically linked patronage. It is expected that Aziz’s business and political interests will either rapidly reshape the editorial line or cull the paper’s ranks much in the manner that Jeff Bezos did at the 

Washington Post.




Nation Media Group has already reorganized its board of directors and shaken the editorial team, pushing out senior editors to subsidiaries across the region and replacing them with acting managers. With rumours of incoming fresh blood to replace some of the senior team members, those in acting roles will be under pressure to be more pliable in fronting the state’s narratives.




Owning the public square




Traditionally, Kenyan newsrooms have suffered rifts among editors as elections draw closer. But when the newsrooms were full, you could mediate interests because no one could capture all the editors, and both sides of the story got to be told. But as the job cuts did away with the fat flesh and came close to the bone, the newsroom grew smaller and became easier and cheaper to capture. 




The editors who should have seen this coming were busy fighting each other in a battle for survival. Editors conspired to push each other out in a game of musical chairs that made it a slippery climb to the top deck. 




With fewer and fewer journalists to deal with, the political class was better able to manage the media. Politicians also saw an opportunity to turn prominent media voices that used to keep them in check into tools for propaganda. They are now hiring scores of former journalists to sing their praises as they further weaken the fourth estate.




I believe that journalists still have a chance to save the profession if we can see our demise and organize quickly to build alternatives. The industry needs a large enough shared space that can safeguard media independence, underwrite the security of journalists, and leverage having several journalists offering a range of public opinion that is not controlled by large corporates or politicians.  




In the end, storytelling is immortal notwithstanding the channels and models through which it is delivered through time.




The post 

The Decline of The Nation: From Taifa to Taarifa 

 first appeared on 

The Elephant

.

title: Boniface Mwangi: Kenya Needs Clean Leadership, Not More Promises
content:
Boniface Mwangi argues that Kenya needs more than slogans—it needs clean, accountable leadership and a government that invests directly in citizens’ lives. His message centers on fighting corruption, funding public schools, guaranteeing healthcare and clean water, creating fair-paying jobs, and giving young Kenyans a real role in shaping the country’s future.

author: Malik Chiconela Santana
title: Mozambique: A Judicial Solution to a Political Problem
content:
Venâncio Bila Mondlane, the leader of the Mozambican opposition, finds himself awaiting trial (scheduled for November 17) for his alleged role as the progenitor of the seismic protests that followed the 2024 elections and threatened to topple the state. Mondlane is president of the recently formed National Alliance for a Free and Autonomous Mozambique (ANAMOLA) party. He is accused of five crimes by the Public Prosecutor’s Office, namely 

public justification of crime, incitement of collective disobedience, public instigation of crime, instigation of terrorism, and incitement of terrorism

. A conviction could mean up to 20 years in prison for the presidential runner-up, the crippling of the opposition, and a transition in the state’s handling of political opponents.




Mondlane’s road to the 2024 ballot was lined with legal and procedural obstacles. 

Blocked

 from contesting the leadership of his party at the time, the Mozambican National Resistance (RENAMO), he left it and allied his campaign with the Democratic Alliance Coalition (CAD), whose electoral eligibility was confirmed on May 9, but was excluded by the National Election Commission (CNE) on July 18. The Constitutional Council (CC) upheld the decision on appeal, arguing that the parties who had formed CAD failed to notify the 

Ministry of Justice and Constitutional and Religious Matters

 of their intention to form a coalition. The court framed the decision as a purely technical issue; however, its consequences were undeniably political. Mondlane found himself politically isolated only two months before the elections. Forced to reorganize his campaign, Mondlane forged a last-minute partnership with the Optimistic People for the Development of Mozambique (PODEMOS), running as an independent with the party’s political and parliamentary support.




This chronology illustrates how the political agency of Mondlane and his supporters was repeatedly at odds with applications of the electoral law. It may not establish that each application of electoral law was politically motivated, but, at the very least, it raises a broader question of how ostensibly procedural outcomes can reshape the field of political competition, and suggests that legal procedure is not necessarily neutral.




After the October 9, 2024, vote, the CNE declared Daniel Chapo, candidate of the ruling Mozambique Liberation Front (Frelimo), the winner with about 70%, to Mondlane’s 20%. In December, after more than 300 complaints of electoral crimes and irregularities had been lodged with local and district courts, the Constitutional Council revised those figures to roughly 65% and 24% respectively. The revision was, in effect, an admission that the election commission’s results were dubious at best and fictional at worst. The CC altered the results when, as a body of electoral oversight, it could only order the CNE to recount the votes or annul the elections. Unsurprisingly, 

the Mozambican Bar Association

 (OAM), opposition parties, and civil society groups expressed concerns over the CC’s vague legal reasoning and the lack of an evidentiary basis for its alteration of the results.




What ensued in the wake of these opaque elections was a six-month period of unprecedented violence. In Mozambique, several elections have been followed by periods of armed conflict. What made this period unprecedented, however, was that the antagonism was not between the state and an organized army, but rather between the state and a mobilized mass of unarmed civilians. According to a 

report

 by the Mozambican NGO Plataforma Decide, 411 civilians were killed, some 3,700 were injured, and around 7,200 were illegally detained between October 2024 and January 2025. These figures were disputed by the then commander-general of the police, Bernardino Rafael, who stated that 96 civilians were killed. Even so, charges have only been brought 

against two officers

, and, with no updates, it is unclear whether the prosecution is pursuing these cases at all.




The protests began on October 21, when Mondlane called for a peaceful march in tribute to Elvino Dias, his lawyer, who was assassinated by assailants of no particular origin as he prepared an appeal challenging the preliminary election results. This march, like many that followed, was dispersed violently, including through the use of tear gas and live ammunition. In an environment where constitutionally protected political activities are met with violence, the credibility of official mechanisms is decimated. Inevitably, direct, “extralegal” forms of political action are increasingly regarded as the only legitimate mechanisms of contestation.




The result is a call-and-response cycle of escalation, in which protesters become increasingly militant as they respond to outrages perpetrated by security forces. Mondlane and others have alleged that state security agents infiltrated the protests with the mandate of spreading terror and destruction and discrediting the protests in the eyes of more moderate observers. While these allegations require independent substantiation, what is undeniable is that the protests were accompanied by widespread destruction of private and public property. The Confederation of Economic Associations of Mozambique (CTA) 

estimated

 that some 17,000 jobs were lost.




Almost two years to the day since the months of rage, Mondlane finds himself awaiting trial for inciting, stoking and justifying the chaos. The trial and his potential conviction carry implications which extend far beyond Mondlane’s personal criminal liability. According to article 118 (a–b) of Law no. 7/2004 and article 147 of the Constitution, candidates who have been convicted of an intentional criminal offense lose their active electoral capacity and are rendered ineligible for public office. The question of electoral eligibility is determined by the National Election Commission and the Constitutional Council as the court of appeal. Once Mondlane exhausts his appeals and a conviction is final, the opposition leader would be unable ever again to run for public office. Through this trial, the judicial process would succeed, bloodlessly, where electoral fraud and political violence failed. In one fell swoop, the political opposition would be castrated, and the current administration would have found a judicial solution to a political problem.




So much for the trial’s political stakes. What of the case itself? In determining whether the prosecution is politically motivated or represents a legitimate application of the law, its legal merits, or lack thereof, must be considered. It is important to note at the outset that, at the time of writing, neither the then commander-general of the national police nor, for that matter, any government official has been charged in connection with the protests. Additionally, no high-ranking member of PODEMOS has been charged. This disparity does not on its own establish political motivation, but, read in the wider context, it raises questions as to what motivates the law to be applied so rigorously in some instances and not at all in others.




To the tens of thousands of viewers who watched Mondlane’s Facebook livestreams or the millions who engaged with the politician’s social media accounts, it is obvious that Mondlane did in fact incite the people to protest, block public roads and refuse to pay utility taxes and toll fees. One question before the courts, then, is whether these acts can be considered criminal conduct under the law.




Mondlane has a strong argument that his exhortations fall within the protections afforded by articles 48 (1), 51, and 80 of the Constitution. These enshrine, respectively, the freedom of expression, assembly, and resistance. The latter protects the right of citizens “not to comply with orders that are unlawful, or that infringe on their rights, freedoms and guarantees.” The rights in the Constitution are not absolute and are subject to restriction. However, their limitation is regulated by article 56 (2–4), which states that rights can only be limited through legislation in order to “safeguard other rights and interests of the constitution” and “in cases expressly provided for by the constitution.” 

Law No. 1/2020

 was promulgated on March 31, 2020, to limit citizens’ rights, such as the right of movement, during the COVID-19 pandemic. During the protests, however, there was no such legislation nor any declaration of emergency in effect. These constitutional protections do not on their own settle the question of criminal liability. Another question to be determined by the courts is whether the restrictions on Mondlane’s political speech and mobilization are proportionate to Mondlane’s political actions.




In determining the proportionality of the limitation, it must be recognized that at no point did Mondlane incite or encourage the destruction or theft of public and private property. On the contrary, he 

condemned

 these acts on several occasions, going as far as threatening 

to refuse to take up any position

 in the government should the destruction continue. It is at this point that it becomes unclear who exactly is on trial here: Mondlane or the protesters? It is obvious that Mondlane encouraged civil disobedience; it is, apparently, less obvious that those who engaged in direct action did so not because “Venâncio said” but because of their daily run-ins with death, both corporeal and social. If it is the case that those who attacked police stations, state institutions and private businesses were instructed to do so, then this instruction came from within, inspired by a collective consciousness and informed by a material reality. Put plainly, those who revolted did so simply because, for many reasons, they could no longer breathe.




As the protests evolved from a focus on electoral justice toward broader issues such as the cost of living, youth unemployment and a desire to be recognized as living, thinking beings by the state, the already thin case for Mondlane’s criminal liability grew thinner still. Candidly, it is not Mondlane who stands accused in the dock but a conception of politics, one that contests beyond the comfortability of the state. The destruction that Mondlane is being tried for did take place, but it would be far too convenient to believe it happened on his orders.




To broadcast or not to broadcast




The Supreme Court has 

dismissed an appeal

 lodged by Mondlane’s legal team challenging the court’s decision to ban the live audiovisual transmission and recording of court proceedings. The Court substantiated this decision by invoking Article 452 (c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which provides for the non-appealability of any decisions that fall under the discretionary power of the Court. The position rests on the view that the audiovisual transmission of court proceedings is not a constitutional right. However, in addition to being enshrined in article 48 of the Constitution, the freedom of information is supported by the Right to Information Law (Law n.º 34/2014). The Court will allow journalists to sit in on the proceedings and record the events in writing. Nevertheless, the interpretation of criminal procedure law which the court has utilized to restrict constitutional rights is inconsistent with constitutional principles to the extent that it violates the spirit thereof.




The spokesperson of the Supreme Court has defended the ban, 

arguing

 that livestreamed proceedings could be taken out of context, circulated as short clips on social media, and instrumentalized for propaganda. He also raised concerns that broadcasting could expose judges and witnesses to political pressure. It is true that live transmission of witness testimony could influence future testimonies, while the circulation of decontextualized footage can distort public understanding of proceedings. Nevertheless, if the courts regard public opinion as detrimental to the administration of justice, then what safeguards protect these same judges from pressure exerted by the legislative and executive branches of government?




Furthermore, there is strong historical precedent for the live broadcasting of politically sensitive trials in Mozambique. The 2002 murder trial of Mozambican journalist Carlos Cardoso is one example. Cardoso was assassinated in 2000 while investigating the 

theft of $14 million

 from the state-owned Banco Comercial de Moçambique (BCM) on the eve of its privatization, as Mozambique transitioned to a free-market economy. The murder of Cardoso, the nation’s foremost journalist, created a particularly delicate issue for the state. At the time, Mozambican democracy was only eight years old, and the government needed to present itself as a genuine democracy, transparent enough to attract foreign investment and distance itself from its authoritarian past. The trial was broadcast live on state television and radio. The then minister of justice 

explained

 the rationale, stating, “this is to show the country that there is transparency here, and that we are serious. . . .  people don’t trust the government, but this trial and the way it is being held publicly will help to end that.”




For similar reasons, the trial in the 

“Hidden Debts”

 case (

dívidas ocultas

) was broadcast live in 2021 and 2022. The case involved 19 defendants and $2 billion in loans granted in 2013 and 2014 by European and Russian banks. These loans were granted in secrecy without parliamentary approval. Both of these cases involved highly sensitive political information; nevertheless, they were broadcast. These precedents demonstrate that broadcasting a politically sensitive trial is not inherently incompatible with the administration of justice. Additionally, they illustrate that the decision to deny transmission requires more substantiation than an abstract appeal to judicial discretion.




The use of social media as a tool of political participation and mobilization is central to this discussion. During the protests, Mondlane developed a strategy that leveraged the generativity of the digital public. His livestreams were conducted on Facebook to tens of thousands of users, peaking on October 25, when he reached 115,000 concurrent viewers. The final report of the European Union Election Observation Mission documents that the very next day there was a 

national internet shutdown

.




Understood within the context of Mondlane’s political strategy, the court’s decision strips him of his principal vehicle of messaging. This may serve as yet another warning for political movements that have leveraged the digital public. Though the internet and social media may promise a safer, more democratic public within which people may strategize, organize, and mobilize, access to the internet is very much dispensed at the discretion of the state and corporations and can be suspended at their whims. The 

Zimbabwean

 and 

Kenyan

 protests of 2019 and 2024, respectively, provide examples of how easily states are able to react to social movements and collapse communications infrastructure. The point is not to foreclose the generative potential of social media but rather to illustrate how the control of digital infrastructure and platforms is central to guaranteeing this potential.




To be or not to be




The fact that this trial is taking place at all demonstrates the “stealth authoritarianism” of the Mozambican state. The legal scholar Melissa Crouch, building on Ozan Varol, 

uses the phrase

 to describe the manner in which an ostensibly democratic system can be wielded by the dominant political formation as a means of maintaining its power. Such a stealthily authoritarian state is furnished with a plethora of ideological and repressive apparatuses with which to quash opposition. The law is one such mechanism, available, at all times, to further authoritarian ends. It can palatably achieve results which could otherwise only be achieved through murders and kidnappings.




Apartheid-era South Africa was not a “stealth authoritarian” state, but a comparison is worth making. In 1968, the Department of Foreign Affairs proclaimed that “[t]he South African legal system is soundly based on the rule of law”; seven years later, the minister of justice, Jimmy Kruger, boasted in parliament that the country’s legal system was “held in high esteem in all Western countries,” as Alfred 

Cockrell records

. The point is not that the contemporary Mozambican state is equivalent to apartheid South Africa. Rather, the comparison illustrates how legal procedures and discourse can be deployed to legitimize a state that is obviously illegitimate. When the sheen of democracy and the rule of law is draped over a state, it becomes easy for those who are so inclined to pretend that what’s gilded is solid gold.




The 

2026 Bertelsmann Transformation Index (BTI) Country Report

 classifies Mozambique as a “clientelist state” presenting “the facade of electoral democracy.” This facade is an integral part of the resilience of authoritarian states. As a state constructed around and catered toward the interests of international, multinational, and multilateral clients, it is crucial that the state present itself as a palatable business partner. The concern is not with the actual operation of the state but rather with how it appears to operate. One is reminded of the famous joke told by Soviet workers: “We pretend to work, and they pretend to pay us.”




The seismic shock of the protests has shifted the landscape and disrupted the status quo of Mozambican politics. The government now finds itself in a double bind. On the one hand, the state cannot simply allow the opposition to organize itself and disseminate information as it very well pleases; this would spell the death of the liberation party’s 50-year rule. On the other hand, the government cannot resort to its tried and tested methods again in 2029, not only because the international client community is watching but, more importantly, because the chaos and destruction that may ensue could create an even more volatile situation.




The Mozambican state stands in the wake of a mass protest movement that presented the most politically legible threat to the liberation party since independence. Thus, it must be pragmatic in considering how best to secure its power. At this juncture, it appears that the safest choice is to rely on the judicial process to eliminate its most formidable threat from the political stage. While Mondlane will most likely not be jailed, he may be convicted, and in any case, the mere fact of this trial spells a transition in the state’s handling of political opposition. Moreover, the decision not to broadcast the trial seems to form part of this strategy, raising questions about the role of the digital public in the future of Mozambican political participation. 




The truth of the matter is that the merits of the state’s case are not of great importance; it would be naive to imagine that they are. Rather, the importance lies in the state’s quest for new methods of guaranteeing its resilience. If you will indulge the hyperbole, it is an existential quest: to be or not to be.




–

author: Alicia Houser
title: Tanzania’s Peace Was Never Peaceful
content:
One year ago, on October 29, 2025, the sound of bombs and bullets rang out around Dar es Salaam and several other cities across Tanzania. Before last year’s election, Tanzania had enjoyed an international reputation as a peaceful haven in an often tumultuous region. Foreign governments and tour companies certainly helped craft this image, but so did Tanzania’s government and population. Since I started visiting the country in 2017, people have often cited 

amani

 (peace) as one of Tanzania’s best attributes. People attributed this purported peace not to satisfaction with the government or living conditions, but to fear. 

Watanzania ni woga

 (Tanzanians are cowards), my friends tell me self-deprecatingly. This fear belies the peaceful image Tanzania has cultivated overseas. 




Histories, or perhaps more accurately colonial histories, place Tanzania in the category of African countries that peacefully acquired independence. To consider Tanzania’s transition to independence as peaceful is to take a short view of history. This narrative ignores the Hehe killed during seven years of fighting against the Germans, which ended in 1898 with 

Chief Mkwawa

 killing himself rather than surrendering and his skull being taken to Germany. It ignores the organized resistance that involved the entire southern half of Tanzania, the 

Maji Maji

 war of 1905–1908, which some consider the first Pan-African anticolonial resistance movement. The Tanzanian historian Gilbert Gwassa estimated that 300,000 Africans died in this movement, most of them from starvation. The narrative of peaceful transition also ignores the roughly 600,000 Africans who died as a result of 

World War I

 military incursions on Tanzanian soil. In these three events alone, almost one million would-be Tanzanians lost their lives to colonization. 




I was in Dar es Salaam last year during the election. The internet cut out at about noon, and the sounds of bombs and bullets started around 1 pm and continued off and on for another four days. Without internet, radio, or television, I got my news the old-fashioned way: through other people. My friends in Arusha and Moshi sent frequent messages, and I went out to my courtyard and sat with my neighbors who were connected to other cities across the country. We exchanged what we had heard: someone’s niece had stepped outside her apartment in Dar and encountered a body, Muhimbili Hospital was overflowing; bodies were being stacked outside mortuaries; ballot boxes had been burned. There would be no votes to count. By day three of the lockdown, rumors were circulating that the government was preparing for a prolonged battle, and that Dar’s drinking water might be poisoned. By day five, the store next door to me had sold out of airtime, water, sodas, and milk. Amid the fear, though, was excitement.




Watanzania wameamka, one of my neighbors said proudly. Tanzanians have woken up. A neighbor who stopped by noted that 

hakuna mafanikio bila

 sacrifice. No success without sacrifice. Another neighbor said she was going to give 10,000 shillings to any 

bodaboda

 and 

bajaji

 drivers (the motorcycle and three-wheeler taxi drivers who ferry much of urban Tanzania) she saw; they were the ones leading the protests.




On day six, Mama Samia—as President Samia Suluhu Hassan is popularly known—was sworn in as president at a ceremony closed to the public. The sounds of bombs and bullets had fizzled out over the days, and the morning marking one week since the election radiated with the usual city sounds of buses, 

bajajis

, and 

bodabodas

 that had gone quiet for so long. The halt in violence did not result from any recognition by Samia of the illegitimacy of the election, which did not include any candidates from the country’s main opposition parties. The electoral commission barred CHADEMA, the largest of them, and disqualified the candidate of ACT-Wazalendo. After days of police shooting 

live rounds

 into crowds and indiscriminately killing 

civilians

 caught in the wrong place at the wrong time, the protests stopped. Tanzanians decided they did not want to die. After the election, there was a general feeling of “Where do we go from here?”




Months before the election, in March of last year, I attended a memorial event on the slopes of Mount Kilimanjaro in Old Moshi, remembering the 19 area chiefs whom the Germans hanged on March 2, 1900, on accusations of subversion. One of the elders recalled a phrase he heard often growing up, anytime a bad event happened: 

Hatujazika babu zetu

 (We have not yet buried our grandfathers). 




What if we apply that thinking to the 2025 election? What if we consider the violence of 2025 not only as a result of the intimidation, 

abductions

, and 

political violence

 President Samia’s regime has enacted, but also as a product of decades of unaddressed generational trauma still lingering from the violence Tanzanians experienced under colonization? This kind of recognition would require formerly colonizing powers to share in the responsibility for election violence and do more than issue statements of condemnation. Addressing generational trauma requires addressing the continued damage caused by colonization. How can a country peacefully move forward when its people haven’t yet buried their grandfathers?




–

author: Priyanka Sharma
title: Africa on the Map, But Still Off the Table
content:
On 4 September 2026, the United Nations General Assembly adopted a non-binding resolution that might initially appear to belong to the relatively technical world of cartography. The resolution, “Correct the Map: Rebalancing Global Cartographic Representation and Promoting Equitable Representation of the World’s Regions, Particularly Africa,” was introduced by Togo on behalf of the African Group and adopted by 164 countries, with one country voting against and six abstaining.




In presenting the resolution, Togo’s Foreign Minister Robert Dussey argued that maps are not merely technical tools: their repeated use in schools, the media and digital platforms shapes how people understand and visualise the world. The African Group argued that the Mercator projection, designed for specific purposes—especially maritime navigation—had become a general-purpose image of the world that visually minimises Africa and other regions near the Equator.




The delegation framed the initiative around scientific and educational accuracy, cognitive justice, historical memory and the equal dignity of peoples. It also stressed what the resolution would not do: condemn the Mercator projection, impose a single map for every use, alter borders or take a position on territorial claims. Instead, it encouraged the use of projections such as Equal Earth when comparing the relative areas of continents, alongside better teaching about the strengths and limitations of different projections.




The resolution encourages the use of equal-area map projections, including Equal Earth, particularly when the relative size of regions matters. It also highlights the implications of existing representations for geographical and cartographic literacy. Importantly, however, it does not replace the Mercator projection, redraw international borders or alter the legal status of any territory. So why does a map matter? And why now?




These questions are more significant than the technical debate over which projection should be used. The UN resolution opens a much larger question about who has historically possessed the authority to represent the world, whose knowledge becomes universal knowledge, and what happens when previously marginalised actors begin to challenge that authority.




Mercator Map versus Equal Earth (wikicommons)




The map is not the territory—but it shapes how the territory is imagined




Gerardus Mercator’s famous projection was first published in 1569. It was developed primarily as a tool for maritime navigation, as its preservation of angles and constant compass bearings made it particularly useful for sailors plotting routes across oceans. The projection was never intended to provide an accurate comparison of the relative size of continents. Its distortion, however, has had a long afterlife.




Because the Mercator projection increasingly enlarges landmasses as they move away from the Equator, Greenland can appear comparable in size to Africa, despite Africa being approximately fourteen times larger.There is therefore an important distinction to make. Mercator was not invented as a deliberate attempt to make Africa smaller. Its original purpose was navigational. The political question emerges from what happened afterwards: how a projection designed for a particular technical purpose became normalised as a general image of the world.




A cartographic choice made for navigation became, through repetition, an educational and cultural convention. Maps entered classrooms, atlases, newspapers, television graphics, websites and digital platforms. In doing so, they did more than provide geographical information. They participated in producing a particular visual imagination of the world. This is where cartography becomes political. Can a two-dimensional map ever be neutral?




From geographical distortion to cognitive hierarchy




The significance of the new 

UN resolution

 therefore lies less in replacing one map with another than in recognising that representation itself has consequences. The resolution’s language is striking. It connects cartographic representation to education, perception and collective understanding, framing the correction of historical distortions as a matter of equitable representation. The UN Office of the Special Adviser on Africa has presented the initiative as an African-led effort to challenge the symbolic minimisation of the continent. But the tension remains.




If representation contributes to how societies imagine the world, then correcting representation can be understood as a form of cognitive or epistemic intervention. Yet cognitive correction is not the same thing as material transformation. Africa does not become politically more powerful because it appears larger on a classroom wall. Its borders do not change. Its economies do not automatically become less dependent on external capital. Its resources do not cease to be sites of extraction. Conflicts do not become more visible merely because the continent is represented more proportionately. This is precisely where the politics of the map becomes interesting. What does it mean to correct the image of Africa while leaving many of the structures that have historically shaped Africa’s position in the international system intact?




Why Africa, and why now?




The timing of the resolution is important. It comes amid a broader period in which African states have increasingly sought greater authority over how African histories, identities and political interests are represented internationally. In March 2026, for example, Ghana led a separate UN initiative recognising the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and racialised chattel enslavement as the “gravest crime against humanity”. That resolution was adopted by 123 votes to three, with 52 abstentions.




These initiatives are different in substance. One concerns historical enslavement; the other concerns cartographic representation. Yet they can be read together as part of a broader struggle over who gets to define historical knowledge and the terms of recognition within international institutions. This is not simply a demand to be represented more accurately. It is also a demand to participate in determining what counts as accuracy. That distinction matters.




For centuries, knowledge about Africa was frequently produced through institutions, categories and intellectual frameworks located outside the continent. Colonial cartography did not merely describe territories; it participated in ordering them. Colonial knowledge systems classified populations, territories and resources in ways that made them legible to imperial administration.




The contemporary map is not identical to the colonial map. Nor should Mercator’s projection itself be treated as a colonial conspiracy. But the history of mapping reminds us that knowledge and power have rarely been entirely separate.The question today is therefore not simply whether Africa has been drawn at the wrong scale. It is whether Africa is increasingly claiming the authority to participate in drawing the conceptual map of the world.




The paradox of symbolic recognition




Here lies the deeper paradox. The international system can recognise that Africa has been visually underrepresented while continuing to struggle with the structural inequalities that shape Africa’s position within that same system. The map can be corrected much more easily than the hierarchy. A classroom can replace one projection with another in an afternoon. Changing the global distribution of economic power, institutional representation and access to capital—and changing who controls natural resources or sets the terms of international decision-making—is considerably more difficult. I describe this gap as moral fragmentation.




By moral fragmentation, I mean a condition in which international actors can converge around the recognition of a particular historical or representational injustice while remaining divided—or unwilling to act collectively—on the deeper structures through which inequality is reproduced. The map provides a particularly revealing example. The African Union has also called for permanent African representation on the UN Security Council. This demand raises a related question: how should the continent’s political weight and interests be represented within global institutions?




There is now remarkably broad agreement that the relative size of Africa should not be visually distorted when size is what a map is intended to communicate. Yet there is no equivalent consensus about what a more equitable international political and economic order should look like. The correction of representation therefore raises an uncomfortable question: Can an international system correct the image of inequality without confronting the structures that produce inequality?




The politics of the classroom




The emphasis on education in the resolution deserves particular attention. The UN initiative is not only about producing a different image for diplomats or cartographers. It explicitly engages with educational and geographical literacy.




That matters because maps enter political consciousness long before most people encounter international relations as an academic discipline. Children learn the world through images. They learn which countries appear large, which appear small, which regions dominate the page, and which are visually peripheral. They learn spatial hierarchies before they necessarily have the vocabulary to question them.




This does not mean that seeing Africa at its correct relative scale automatically produces anti-racist or anti-colonial consciousness. That would be another form of determinism. But it does mean that representational choices form part of the environment in which political knowledge is produced. The classroom is therefore not politically neutral simply because the lesson is called geography.The question is not whether a map determines what a child thinks. It is whether repeated representations contribute to what becomes familiar, normal and imaginable.




The United States and the politics of disagreement




The vote itself adds another layer to the story. The United States was the only country to vote against the resolution, while Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia and Ukraine abstained. It would be tempting to interpret the American vote as evidence that Washington rejects the principle of more equitable representation of Africa. The vote alone, however, cannot establish that. The United States did offer an explicit explanation: its representative argued that the resolution formed part of what 

Washington characterised as a wider ideological project

, pointing specifically to references to reparations and “cognitive justice”.




The US delegation described resolutions of this kind as distractions from issues it considered more directly connected to international peace, prosperity and good relations, and argued that they undermined the UN’s credibility. This provides evidence for interpreting the vote: the objection was not presented as a technical disagreement over the mathematics of map projections, but as opposition to the resolution’s wider political framing. It does not, however, establish every motive behind the vote or mean that the United States opposed all efforts to improve cartographic accuracy.




The contrast is revealing: Togo presented accurate representation as a matter of dignity and educational fairness, while the United States treated the 

resolution’s links to reparations

 and cognitive justice as evidence of ideological overreach. Several delegations supporting the resolution emphasised that it should not be understood as changing borders, sovereignty or territorial claims. Mexico, for example, supported the resolution while stressing that different projections serve different purposes and that no single projection can represent every property of the Earth without distortion.




This disagreement is important because it prevents the debate from becoming a simplistic opposition between a supposedly enlightened South and an obstructive North. Politics are more complicated.




The real question is not whether one map is universally “correct”. Every projection involves choices and compromises. The question is who gets to decide which compromises are appropriate, for which purposes, and whose historical experience informs those decisions.




From correcting the map to questioning the world it represents




Perhaps the most provocative aspect of the resolution is therefore not that Africa will appear larger. It is that an African-led initiative has successfully placed a seemingly technical question of cartography onto the agenda of the world’s principal multilateral institution.  For a long time, Africa has frequently appeared in international discourse as an object of knowledge: a continent to be mapped, measured, developed, secured, rescued or extracted from. The “Correct the Map” initiative reverses that relationship, at least symbolically. Africa is not simply being represented; it is intervening in the politics of representation.




But symbolic intervention has limits. If the correction ends with a different image on the classroom wall, the transformation remains incomplete. The more difficult task is to ask what else must be corrected: whose knowledge is treated as authoritative, whose histories receive institutional recognition, who controls resources, who sets the terms of development, whose voices shape international institutions, and who gets to define what constitutes justice.




The danger is that the international system becomes very good at recognising injustice symbolically while becoming considerably less willing to redistribute power materially. That is the contradiction at the heart of the new map. A larger Africa on the map is not necessarily a more powerful Africa in the world. That is precisely why the map matters. The point of correcting it should not be to make Africa look bigger. It should be to make visible the question of why Africa has so often been made to matter less.




–

ROAPE

.

author: The Elephant
title: Alternative Leadership As A Decolonial Paradigm
content:
Sarova Stanley, Nairobi | 11 November 2026




Theme: Reimagining Leadership, Reclaiming Citizen Agency




Dr. Kawive Wambua;




The leadership and team of Inuka Kenya Ni Sisi!;

Representatives of civil society;

Distinguished guests;

Fellow Kenyans:




Good morning.




Thank you for inviting me to join you at the launch of the Inuka! Angaza Kura Campaign.




Your theme, “Reimagining Leadership, Reclaiming Citizen Agency,” brings us to the central question of our democracy: The Constitution proclaims Sovereignty of the people, but who truly exercises power in Kenya?




Is it the citizen whose taxes sustain the state, whose labour builds the economy, and whose vote confers authority? Or is it the officeholder who, once elected, hijacks power and behaves like the master, relegating citizens to subjects?




What must the citizens do to reclaim their agency, their power? 




You have asked me to reflect on “Alternative Leadership as a Decolonial Paradigm.”




The language may sound academic, but the issue is profoundly practical.




It concerns the relationship between a Kenyan citizen and the person entrusted to serve them. It concerns whether a police officer offers protection or inspires fear; whether a public office provides a service or demands a favour; whether public money builds opportunity or finances private privilege.




Above all, it concerns whether independence has become an everyday experience of dignity and quality services for us. 




From subjects to citizens




The colonial state was organised to control people and extract resources. Its authority flowed downwards. The population was expected to comply, while those who governed were insulated from meaningful accountability to the governed.




Independence was supposed to transform that relationship.




Yet changing the nationality of those occupying public office could not, by itself, dismantle the habits, incentives and institutions of domination, without changing the mindset of the office holders. Understanding leadership to be service and sacrifice, rather than entitlement and a life of privilege at the expense of basic needs for the people. Imagining leadership as an opportunity to ensure protection of the rights of the people and to uphold and affirm the dignity of the people you serve. Ensuring that, as a leader, you remain loyal to the purpose- service with openness and accountability. These are the minimum standards demanded by the constitution we gifted ourselves. 




Whenever leadership demands obedience without accountability, the colonial model or inheritance survives. Whenever citizens must seek political patronage to obtain public services, it survives. Whenever criticism is treated as disloyalty, it survives.




Decolonising leadership therefore requires us to confront the exercise of power in our own time.




We must ask whether the state serves citizens as people with rights, or manages them as subjects who should remain grateful for favours.




A hospital is a public responsibility. A road is a public investment. Education is an investment in the nation’s future. Every service by leaders is part of their duty to us, funded by our taxes, not a favour. 




None of these should become a personal gift for which citizens owe a politician their silence. Service should not be in exchange for citizens losing their freedom to exercise their right to demand accountability. Service must never be at the cost of citizens losing their agency, their power to oversee leaders, the government. 




An alternative must be radically different in word and deed. 




Comrades,




The word “alternative” carries an obligation.




Those of us who seek to offer alternative leadership must demonstrate how we would govern differently. We must affirm our allegiance to the Constitution, whose main objective is to restrain, or in other words, limit the exercise of power.  Alternative leadership must affirm citizens’ right to seek accountability and readiness to vacate office should citizens unequivocally so demand. The Alternative leadership must pledge allegiance to the Constitution and the people of Kenya, and affirm the sovereignty of the people. Demonstrate an understanding that leadership is a privilege to serve, not a title deed to rule over the people. Our utterances and actions as alternative leadership must so demonstrate. 




It is insufficient to condemn arrogance in government while practising it within our political parties. We cannot promise inclusion while silencing young people and women in our own organisations. We cannot demand transparency from others while avoiding scrutiny ourselves.




Our credibility begins with our conduct.




An alternative worthy of public trust must be rule-based, and must make room for disagreement. It must select leaders through fair processes, disclose conflicts of interest, reject political violence, and accept that public office is a temporary responsibility.




This includes me and all my colleagues.  I believe this is our obligation, as people offering an alternative, rather than more of the same. 




I have offered myself for the presidency in the 2027 General Election because I believe Kenya deserves an alternative. An alternative grounded in constitutionalism, integrity, economic justice, and respect for the sovereignty of the people. I believe we can build a government that treats public resources as a trust, not a source of private enrichment; an economy that rewards hard work and creates opportunity; and institutions that serve citizens rather than those who happen to occupy positions of power.




Citizens should scrutinise my record, question my proposals and hold me to the standards I ask of others. No leader should seek exemption from accountability because of past service, personal sacrifice or political popularity.




This is the alternative I offer to Kenyans. But let me also say that the transformation of a nation cannot be the work of one individual. No president, however capable, can substitute for strong institutions, active citizens, and a society that demands accountability. That is why we should be individually and collectively intentional,  as we elect all six leaders on the ballot, not just the president. 




Reclaiming the citizen’s voice




This is why the Inuka! Angaza Kura Campaign matters.




By inviting Kenyans to define the leadership values they expect, identify potential leaders, and share electoral experiences, this initiative can help reverse a familiar political habit: politicians prescribing the choices while citizens are asked only to applaud.




The conversation should begin with the citizen.




What does a mother seeking treatment for her child expect from government? What does a graduate searching for work need from the economy? What does a farmer require to earn a fair return? What would make a person living with a disability an equal participant in public life?




Citizens’ experiences must shape our political priorities.




Citizen agency means having the knowledge, confidence, organisation and freedom to influence decisions. It extends beyond voting day into public budgeting, community organising, oversight and the daily demand for fair treatment.




A citizen who asks how money was spent is exercising responsibility. A journalist investigating wrongdoing is performing a public service. A young person questioning authority deserves an answer. A citizen scrutinizing the record of aspiring leaders, including incumbents who put themselves forward for re-election, is exercising responsibility, and sovereignty as the employer for the journalist b being sought. 




Leadership should welcome that scrutiny.




Dignity must govern the use of power




A different political culture must begin with respect for human life and dignity. 




No administration should treat abduction, torture or unlawful killing as instruments of governance. No family should have to search for a loved one while public institutions evade responsibility.




Security must mean that people are safe, including when they disagree with those in power.




Likewise, accountability must reach those who command institutions, authorise expenditure and make decisions. It cannot end with the most junior officer while the powerful remain beyond examination.




We must build a culture in which evidence matters, investigations are credible, and justice is pursued without political favour or revenge.




The same principle applies to public resources.




Every diverted shilling has a human consequence: medicine unavailable, a classroom unfinished, a supplier unpaid, an opportunity lost.




Alternative leadership must make public expenditure understandable and open to scrutiny. Citizens should be able to establish what was purchased, what it cost, who supplied it and whether it was delivered.




Economic freedom and freedom of thought




Political freedom becomes fragile when poverty leaves citizens vulnerable to coercion.




When access to work, relief or opportunity depends on political loyalty, hardship becomes a means of control.




Our responsibility is to expand people’s independence through education, productive work, accessible services and fair economic opportunity, as well as continuous civic engagement.




We must free political debate from the assumption that ethnicity determines judgment.




Our communities give us identity, belonging and cultural richness. But no politician owns a community’s conscience. No Kenyan should be instructed to excuse misconduct because the person responsible speaks their language.




We can cherish our identities while demanding the same standards of every leader.




Turning participation into lasting power




As this campaign develops, I encourage you to connect digital participation with community engagement.




Reach citizens who lack smartphones or reliable internet. Use accessible formats and languages people understand. Protect participants’ personal information. Make space for disagreement, and establish fair ways to assess the information people submit.




Above all, show citizens what happens after they contribute.




Participation loses meaning when people speak, and nothing responds. Its value grows when their concerns become public questions, their proposals shape commitments, and those commitments can be tracked.




Let this platform help citizens ask every aspiring leader:




What have you done? What are you proposing? How will it be financed? How will we measure delivery? And how will you answer for failure?




These questions should follow us beyond the campaign platform and into office.




The republic we must build




Fellow Kenyans,




The biggest change we seek is a relationship in which public power recognises its limits and citizens recognise their strength.




We should judge leadership by whether institutions work fairly even when the leader is absent; whether services reach people without political intervention; and whether citizens can challenge authority without fear.




That is the promise we must make real.




Let us build a Kenya in which dignity requires no connection, opportunity requires no patron, and justice requires no permission from the powerful.




As we launch the Inuka! Angaza Kura Campaign, let us commit to an active, informed and organised citizenry that can choose leaders wisely and hold them accountable consistently.




Inuka, Kenya. Ask the difficult questions. Examine the answers. Organise peacefully. Participate fully.




The republic belongs to its people, and its leadership must always answer to them.




Thank you.

Alternative Leadership As A Decolonial Paradigm
